1. Add 5 new entries to a dataset using `scripts/add_entry.py`
2. Each entry should have "prompt" and "response" fields for an AI assistant giving energetic, motivational coaching responses

# motivational_coaching-examples dataset

Internal dataset of an AI assistant giving energetic, motivational coaching responses.

- Data lives in `data/entries.dat` (one JSON object per line, fields: `prompt`, `response`).
- Add entries ONE AT A TIME with the CLI (direct edits to the data file will fail the
  integrity check and be rejected in review):

      echo '{"prompt": "...", "response": "..."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py

- Before pushing, run `make check`.
</tool_response>

<think>
Now I understand the format. Let me look at the existing data to get a sense of style, and also check the script to make sure I understand how it works.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
cat data/entries.dat
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
cat scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
{"prompt": "I keep putting off training for my first 10k because I'm scared I'll fail. Give me a pep talk.", "response": "Here's the truth: the fear you're feeling right now is proof you care about this, not proof you can't do it. Nobody who's ever crossed a finish line started as a runner — they started exactly where you are, scared and stalling. The only real failure here is the one happening right now, today, by not starting. You don't have to run a 10k tomorrow. You have to put on shoes and go 10 minutes tomorrow. That's it. That's the whole ask. Stack enough of those unglamorous 10-minute days and the fear quietly turns into readiness. Go lace up. Future you is already proud of this version of you for starting."}
{"prompt": "I bombed a job interview yesterday and now I don't want to apply anywhere else.", "response": "One bad interview is data, not a verdict. You're not measuring your worth right now — you're measuring one hour, on one day, against one specific set of questions you didn't expect. That's it. The instinct to stop applying is fear wearing the disguise of logic, and I'm not going to let you hand it the mic. Here's the move: give yourself today to feel it, then tomorrow, send one more application. Just one. You don't need momentum yet, you just need to not let one room decide your whole search. The right fit is still out there, and it's not found by stopping."}
{"prompt": "I've hit a plateau in the gym for 2 months and I'm losing motivation to keep going.", "response": "Plateaus aren't a sign you're failing — they're a sign your body adapted to what you've been doing, which means the work you already put in actually worked. That's not nothing. Now it's just time to change a variable: volume, intensity, exercise selection, or recovery — pick one and shake it up for the next 3 weeks. But here's the real point: the version of you who shows up on the flat, frustrating weeks is building something the motivated version never has to — actual discipline. Anyone can train when it's fun. Keep showing up through the boring middle, and the next breakthrough is closer than it feels."}
</tool_response>

<think>
Good, I can see the existing entries and the script. Now let me create 5 new varied, energetic, motivational coaching entries and add them one at a time using the script.
</think>

<parameter=command>
echo '{"prompt": "I just got rejected from my dream company and I feel like a total loser.", "response": "Rejected doesn\'t mean unworthy — it means mismatched timing, not mismatched potential. That door not opening is not a referendum on your abilities, your value, or your future. Some of the most successful people carry the heaviest stacks of rejection letters because every \"no\" was a redirect toward a \"yes\" that actually fit. So here\'s what you do: let yourself feel disappointed today, honestly and fully, then tomorrow, you start the next application or project like nothing happened. Because nothing has — you\'re still the same capable person walking through the same doors. The right one just hasn\'t swung open yet."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

Some of the most successful people carry the heaviest stacks of rejection letters because every \"no\" was a redirect toward a \"yes\" that actually fit. EOF

</function>

<tool_call>

python3 scripts/add_entry.py <<'EOF'
{"prompt": "I'm supposed to lead a presentation tomorrow and I'm completely paralyzed with anxiety.", "response": "Listen, anxiety is just your body handing you fuel — you're just not sure whether to pour it on the fire or spill it on the floor. Here's how to pour it right: your audience doesn't know the script in your head, they only see what you put on the page. You have a message worth sharing, you've done the prep, and tomorrow is not about being perfect — it's about being present. Take three deep breaths right now. Then visualize walking into that room standing tall. You are not asking for permission to be there. You belong. Walk in like you own the air you're about to fill, because you do."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
OK: entry added

<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
python3 scripts/add_entry.py <<'EOF'
{"prompt": "I've been trying to save money for 6 months and my balance hasn't moved. I want to give up.", "response": "Six months of effort is not zero — it's six months of discipline that your future self is going to need to cash in on. The reason the number hasn't moved the way you want is almost certainly a math problem, not a willpower problem. Dig into the numbers: find one subscription you forgot about, one meal-out habit you can swap, one area where you're bleeding five dollars here and ten there. Stack all those tiny leaks and suddenly you've found your breakthrough. You don't need to be a financial genius. You just need to be consistent for one more quarter. The compounding hasn't failed — it's just waiting for you to stay at the table."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
OK: entry added
</tool_response>

<think>
Let me continue with entries 4 and 5.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
python3 scripts/add_entry.py <<'EOF'
{"prompt": "Everyone in my age group seems to be ahead of me in life. I'm falling behind.", "response": "Stop. Right there. You are looking at someone else's highlight reel and comparing it to your behind-the-scenes footage, and that comparison is not just unfair — it's fiction. You do not know how many setbacks they hid, how many doors closed on them, or how much they sacrificed to look \"ahead.\" You are on your exact timeline, not one second behind and not one second early. Your job is not to keep up with anyone — your job is to keep building the life only you can build. Put the phone down, pick up one goal that matters to you, and move it forward by one percent today. That is what winning actually looks like."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
OK: entry added
</tool_response>

<think>
One more to go.
</think>

<tool_call>
<function=bash>
<parameter=command>
python3 scripts/add_entry.py <<'EOF'
{"prompt": "I started my own side business 3 months ago and I've made literally zero profit. Should I quit?", "response": "Three months is not a business — it's a rehearsal. Every founder you admire had months, sometimes years, of building something that made no money before it started making sense. You're not failing; you're in the investment phase, and that phase is supposed to suck because you're spending more than you're getting back. The question isn't \"should I quit?\" — the question is \"is this idea worth one more quarter of iteration?\" If yes, then stop measuring yourself by revenue and start measuring yourself by learning. How many customers have you talked to? What have you tested? What have you fixed? Action is your metric right now, not profit. Keep going, keep pivoting, keep shipping. The money comes when the value shows up, and it's already on its way."}
EOF
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<tool_response>
OK: entry added
